title: The homemade oven incubator
summary: The clinic doctor and nurse built an incubator on the stove for the 2-1/4 pound baby, who stayed in hospital six weeks while she supplied her milk.

blocks.x: Finally, when they came, which I guess -- well, as I say, I have no idea how long it was. It wasn't too long, that I can tell you, because now they weren't as busy then as they would be now, you know. I don't even know if this type of thing would have even happened now. If something like this happened I would have to be rushed to the hospital immediately. I didn't

even get to the hospital, didn't get to go to the hospital. So when they came, she says, "Oh, come up." You know, we lived upstairs where you pressed the button and the button opens the door. She says, "Come in quick. Come in quick, she's had the baby." "She's had the baby?" And they ran upstairs, this doctor and this nurse ran up the steps. "Oh, my, my, she's had the baby." So they came in immediately, and when they saw the baby and he was still alive and, you know, he was a little fellow, 2-1/4 pounds. Then they got busy, and they started asking me about the pans or something. I said, "Whatever you see in there that you want to use, use it."

So what they had to do was to make an incubator, you know. They had to prepare an incubator, and this they did. They prepared this incubator and put him, you know --they cleaned him up and put him in the incubator, and in the meantime they gave me -- the doctor -- well, he was so busy working on the baby he didn't do too much to me right then, but then they gave me a shot, you know, they gave me a shot. And they worked on him and got him all straightened and put him in this pot on top -- you know, made this homemade incubator.
How was the homemade incubator made?

Well, they sat it on top of the oven. They lighted the oven, you see. See, you didn't have the -- if this had happened today, because I have a modern -- I have a real modern stove today, you know, with the oven and the broiler

underneath, this type of thing, you know. But at that time you just had a flat topped stove, see, where the burners were on one side and the oven was on the other side, see. So on the side where the oven was, well that's what -- they lighted that oven and sat this big pot there and they had blankets -- they had a big blanket and they cleaned him and did whatever they were supposed to do to him and placed him in this -- and this is the homemade incubator.

No doubt if it had been even at a time when it was cold, he probably wouldn't have made it, you know, because he probably would have been exposed to the cold weather. But it was hot. It was warm. Not exceedingly hot, but it was warm. The 15th of June, you can imagine.

So they kept him in this incubator and took him on out to the hospital, and he stayed hospitalized I guess about -- in this incubator -- about six weeks before he gained normal weight. And at that time, you know, you used to stay about two weeks before you really felt free to get out. Nowadays you can get out in the next 24 hours.

And I -- when I went to the hospital, after the first two weeks -- oh, and I breast fed him. I mean I, you know, kept him alive with milk, with my milk, and they told me and told my husband, well take all the milk, get all the milk she can get for the baby. So I did have an awful lot of
milk at that time and he would take the milk out there to see him.
